Testimony of Rep. David Boyer introducing
LD 1360, An Act to Preserve Traditional Driver's Licenses and Nondriver
Identification Cards
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Transportation April 15, 2025

Senator Nangle, Representative Crafts, and esteemed members of the Committee on
Transportation, my name is Rep. David Boyer, and I am proud to present LD 1360, An Act to
Preserve Traditional Driver's Licenses and Nondriver Identification Cards.
This bill would preserve Maine citizens` choice on whether they would like a REAL ID
compliant identification card. Mainers value their privacy, and this legislation is a recognition
that many Mainers have no plan to obtain a REAL ID.
In today's world, identification is essential, yet not every resident has the same needs. For those
who travel frequently or require access to federal buildings, a REAL ID compliant license is
critical, and this bill ensures they can obtain one. However, many others--those who don't travel
by air or who rarely interact with federal facilities---may not need a REAL ID. This legislation
respects that diversity by offering both options, allowing Maine residents to choose the
identification that best fits their lifestyle.
While an alternative is still being offered by our Secretary of State, this issue is important enough
that the alternative should be enshrined in our law. We use our IDs for many things every day:
driving, picking up prescriptions, conducting financial transactions, and more. Requiring
Mainers to get a REAL ID for these activities is overly restrictive and burdensome. What policy
goals are being realized by forcing this?
This legislation is a practical and principled response to a complex issue. It preserves Maine
citizens' choice, respects their privacy, and avoids the unnecessary burden of mandating REAL
ID for everyday life.

District 87

Testimony in Support of LD 1360: "An Act to Preserve Traditional Driver's Licenses and Nondriver Identification Cards"
Senator Nangle, Representative Crafts, and the distinguished members of the Committee on Transportation, my name is Harris Van Pate, and I serve as policy analyst for Maine Policy Institute. Maine Policy is a free market think tank, a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization that advocates for individual liberty and economic freedom in Maine. Thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony in support of LD 1360, "An Act to Preserve Traditional Driver's Licenses and Nondriver Identification Cards."
This bill reaffirms Mainers' right to choose identification that does not comply with the federal REAL ID Act of 2005 while ensuring their IDs remain valid for all state purposes.
Maine Policy Institute has consistently advocated against unnecessary federal mandates that infringe on state sovereignty and individual privacy. The REAL ID Act, passed under the pretense of national security, created a de facto national identification system that raises serious concerns around data collection, surveillance, and the long-term expansion of federal authority into areas traditionally managed by states.
Requiring biometric data, centralized databases, and expanded document verification protocols, REAL ID poses risks to the privacy and security of every citizen. Even the Department of Homeland Security's 2009 Secretary Napolitano has admitted that the REAL ID system was "unrealistic," "inflexible," and unquestionably more expensive.1 States like Maine, which initially rejected the program, were right to be skeptical.
LD 1360 recognizes that many Mainers--particularly senior citizens, those in rural communities, and those with privacy concerns--do not need or want a federally compliant ID. This bill preserves choice by ensuring access to a non-REAL ID option for driver's licenses and identification cards. It prevents Mainers from being forced into a federalized identification regime simply to satisfy arbitrary documentation rules.
This approach is consistent with the principles of limited government and individual autonomy. It also mirrors actions taken in other states. For example, New Hampshire,2 Minnesota,3 and Missouri4 have all taken steps to offer non-compliant identification options in response to public demand for privacy-friendly alternatives.

TESTIMONY OF MICHAEL KEBEDE, ESQ. LD 160 - Ought to Pass
LD 1360 - Neither for Nor Against
An Act to Eliminate REAL ID Requirements in Maine
An Act to Preserve Traditional Driver's Licenses and Nondriver Identification Cards
Joint Standing Committee on Transportation April 15, 2025
Senator Nangle, Representative Crafts, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Transportation, greetings. My name is Michael Kebede, and I am Policy Director at the ACLU of Maine, a statewide organization committed to advancing and preserving civil rights and civil liberties guaranteed by the Maine and U.S. Constitutions. On behalf of our members, we urge you to support LD 160. We are neither for nor against LD 1360, which, although intended to give Maine residents a non-REAL-ID option, might still expose them to the privacy risks of the REAL ID system.
If enacted, LD 160 would repeal the law that empowers the Secretary of State to issue identification cards that are compliant with the federal REAL ID Act of 2005.1 LD 1360 would ensure that Maine residents who want an ID that is not compliant with the REAL ID Act can always obtain one from the Secretary of State.
Background
The REAL ID Act (or "the Act") was passed by Congress as part of an Iraq War/Tsunami relief supplemental funding bill in May 2005. The U.S. Senate did not hold even a single hearing on the bill. REAL ID imposes a burdensome set of requirements on states as part of its aim to turn Americans' driver's licenses into a national identity card system.
In January 2007, Maine became the first state in the nation to reject the REAL ID Act when an overwhelming bipartisan majority of the 123rd Legislature supported an anti-REAL ID resolution.2 Over 20 other states followed suit in pushing back as a rebellion against REAL ID took off across the country. In 2017, faced with growing federal determination to impose

Threat to Privacy
REAL ID makes us all less safe by creating the illusion of security, while doing nothing to truly protect us from danger. It exposes all Americans to an increased danger of identity theft and fraud. It turns a document designed to ensure that only qualified drivers get behind the wheel into a domestic passport.
The REAL ID Act mandates that states include certain features on each driver's license or identity card that the state issues, and it requires that states collect and store vast amounts of personal information about people who apply for identification cards. The Act also requires states to retain a digital scan of source identity documents like birth certificates or passports for at least l0 years (or a paper copy for 7 years). That means a BMV worker must scan and store source documents for each applicant.
In perhaps its most invasive requirement, Title II, Section 202(d)(12) of the Act requires all states to "[p]rovide electronic access to all other States to information contained in the motor vehicle database of the State."4 This means that even if LD 1360 was enacted and Maine continued issuing identification cards that do not comply with the REAL ID Act, the Act would require the Secretary of State to give the federal government access to information linked to those ID cards. For this reason, we are neither for nor against LD 1360 because it could give Maine residents the false belief that their data is safer than it is. We urge the committee to investigate whether there is a way to amend this bill to protect data of people who hold a non-REAL ID.
Threats to Religious Freedom and the Right to Travel
The REAL ID Act burdens Americans' constitutional right to travel, which the U.S. Supreme Court has recognized.5 Indeed, the right to travel is so strong that it is "assertable against private interference as well as governmental action ... a virtually unconditional personal right, guaranteed by the Constitution to us all."6
Moreover, the REAL ID Act's requirement, without any exemption, that a digital photograph appear on each identification card, violates the religious beliefs of several religious groups. It forces the Amish, Mennonites, Muslim

The regulations state that to receive a REAL ID, every applicant must have a photo taken. While the regulations acknowledge religious objections, they do not offer a real solution to this constitutional problem instead they assert that states can provide religious objectors with non-REAL ID compliant licenses. Conclusion REAL ID is an apt illustration of the adage that "those who trade a little liberty for a little security will lose both." REAL ID is a misguided approach to keeping American's safe. Building systems to track, monitor, and judge the lives of every resident will only jeopardize our privacy and expose us to new dangers. REAL ID does not make us safer, it only makes us less free. Moreover, no Maine resident should be forced to choose between their religious beliefs and the need to use an ID card to freely move about the country, enter a federal building, and operate in society in a myriad of other ways. We urge you to vote for LD 160 and consider amending LD 1360 to protect Maine people's privacy from REAL ID tracking if they elect to have a nonREAL ID.

JOINT STANDING COMMITTEE ON TRANSPORTATION L.D. 1360 "An Act to Preserve Traditional Driver's Licenses and Nondriver Identification Cards"
Testimony of Shenna Bellows, Secretary of State and Cathie Curtis, Deputy Secretary for the Bureau of Motor Vehicles,
Department of the Secretary of State
Tuesday, April 15, 2025

Senator Nangle, Representative Crafts, Members of the Transportation Committee, I am providing testimony neither for nor against L.D. l360 "An Act to Preserve Traditional Driver's Licenses and Nondriver Identification Cards" and to provide you with information that may be useful to you.
As written, L.D. 1360 would not incur any process, program or fiscal burden upon the Bureau of Motor Vehicles. Indeed, it does nothing that the Secretary of State does not already do. Every day, we issue
driver licenses and ID cards that are not REAL IDs to those Mainers who do not choose a REAL ID. We
wouldn't want to suggest that anything in current law prevents us from doing so.
While that responsibility certainly already exists in the current edition of Title 29-A, our Department
does recognize and support the sponsor's intent to ensure a federal credential standard----such as REAL ID---would not become mandatory in the future. An alternative or standard license or identification card
is an important option to preserve for Mainers, in terms of both financial cost and documentation
requirements. We do not object to this bill, which adds new language to reinforce the Bureau's existing
authority to issue non-REAL ID licenses and identification cards to Mainers up on request.
Thank you for your time and consideration. If the committee has any questions, I'd be more than happy to answer them or conduct the appropriate research. I will be available for the work session.
